title: Why you should stop predicting customer churn and start using uplift models
harvard_reference: Devriendt, F., Berrevoets, J. and Verbeke, W. (2021) 'Why you should stop predicting customer churn and start using uplift models', Information Sciences, 548, pp. 497-515. doi:10.1016/j.ins.2019.12.075.
abstract_summary: The authors argue that uplift modelling (estimating the change in a customer's churn probability caused by a retention action) is a better basis for retention targeting than conventional churn prediction, but note the literature lacked a direct, like-for-like comparison. They introduce the maximum profit uplift (MPU) measure, extending the maximum profit (MP) measure used for churn-prediction models, together with a 'liftup' curve and measure as uplift counterparts of lift. Using data from a European financial institution's retention campaign (c. 200,903 customers; treatment group churn 13.25% vs control 25.52%), they build logistic-regression and random-forest churn-prediction (CCP) and churn-uplift (CCU) models. Evaluated with MPU, uplift models outperform prediction models: CCP models tend to rank 'lost causes' and 'sure things' highly, whereas CCU models pick out 'persuadables', producing a larger churn reduction and higher campaign profit. The authors conclude uplift modelling is the superior paradigm for data-driven retention, while calling for validation in other application domains.

claims_supported.claim: Uplift models that estimate the incremental effect of a retention action outperform conventional churn-prediction models for retention targeting.
claims_supported.where: Directly stated. Highlights: 'Customer churn uplift models are found to outperform customer churn prediction models.' Abstract, final sentence: uplift models outperform predictive models and improve the profitability of retention campaigns. Section 2.2.1, Eq. (1) defines uplift as P(churn | not treated) minus P(churn | treated), i.e. the incremental effect of the retention action. Section 4.3.1 (Profit curves): evaluated with the MPU measure, 'CCU models outperform CCP models'. Section 4.3.2 (Churn rates): CCP models select many lost causes whereas CCU models target persuadables, giving a larger churn reduction and higher returns, for both logistic regression and random forests. Section 5 (Conclusions): 'customer churn uplift models outperform customer churn prediction models' and 'uplift modeling is a superior paradigm to predictive modeling in the context of supporting customer retention efforts'. Caveats to state in the report: the evidence is one case study at a single European financial institution (not telecom) over a three-month window; under the conventional MP measure the churn-prediction models look better and the uplift advantage appears when the authors' MPU measure is used (Section 4.3.1); the authors themselves say further evidence across more application types is needed (Section 5).

claims_supported.claim: Uplift modelling requires data from randomised retention campaigns (treatment and control groups).
claims_supported.where: Supported in substance for the treatment-and-control requirement; one wording caveat. Section 1.2: uplift modelling 'requires the availability of data that captures the behavior of the modeled system under varying conditions and decision-making scenarios', such data 'may need to be actively collected by setting up experiments', and 'setting up control groups and collecting unbiased data' is what makes uplift modelling possible. Section 2.2.1: 'We assume that a sample of customers is divided into two groups defined as the treatment and control groups' (exposed vs not exposed to the campaign), with the treatment indicator T entering the uplift definition in Eq. (1). Section 4.1.2 (Methodology): the uplift (CCU) model is trained on data sampled from both the treatment and control groups, whereas the prediction (CCP) model uses only the control group. Section 4.3.1: 'it is only possible to calculate the MPU measure if both control and treatment groups are present, which is not the case in traditional customer churn prediction setups.' CAVEAT: the paper never uses the word 'randomised' for how customers are assigned to treatment vs control; it speaks of 'experiments', 'control groups' and 'unbiased data', and describes the case-study data only as a targeted group and a non-targeted group (the only 'random' assignment mentioned is the random stratified train/test split). To cite this source precisely, phrase the claim as 'uplift modelling requires experimental campaign data containing both a treated group and an untreated control group (Devriendt et al., 2021)'. If the report wants to state explicitly that assignment must be randomised, pair it with a second source that says so (to be verified separately).

caveats: Single case study at one European financial institution (contract-termination churn), not telecommunications; c. 200,903 customers, 162 variables, three-month outcome window. Only two learners (logistic regression, random forests) were compared. The uplift advantage is demonstrated under the authors' own MPU measure; under the conventional MP measure the churn-prediction models appear better. The paper does not use the word 'randomised' for treatment assignment. Not applicable to the Kaggle Telco dataset directly, because that dataset contains no treatment/control indicator, so the paper is best cited for the conceptual argument (why churn-probability ranking is not the same as retention targeting) and as a limitation/future-work source.
